column3: Evil consequences strike the doers and the mocked warning encloses them, closely paralleling punishment returning upon its makers.
It directly repeats the disclosure of evil deeds and the enclosing return of what was mocked, strongly clarifying the focus's reversal.
The beautification of evil deeds provides only a remote antecedent to the plotters' eventual punishment.
It names Pharaoh's people and the evil punishment they imposed, a direct historical contrast to the punishment enclosing them in the focus.
The believing man's entrusting his affair to God immediately precedes God's protection of him from their plot.
Remaining mindful of God until death is a broad preventive counterpart to the focus's delivered believer.
The same formula of evil deeds appearing and mocked punishment enclosing their authors is direct but redundant after 16:34 and 45:33.
The arrogant acknowledge that all are within the Fire under God's judgment, extending the punishment scene after the focus.
The evil circle and Hell prepared for those with evil assumptions express a comparable return of evil upon its holders.
It recalls Pharaoh's people's evil punishment of Israel, the oppression whose reversal is implicit in the focus.
The call to be mindful of God offers a general alternative to the wrongdoing that led to Pharaoh's punishment.
Facing evil punishment on the Day of Resurrection gives a close image of failed protection and deserved recompense.
Their great plotting supplies a concise parallel to the plot from which the believer was protected.
The angels' prayer for entry into the Garden provides the positive outcome opposed to the evil punishment in the focus.
It denies efficacy to repentance delayed until death and assigns painful punishment, sharpening the finality of belated wrongdoing.
This repeated account of Pharaoh's people inflicting evil punishment on Israel supplies historical contrast, now redundant with 2:49.
Pharaoh's attempt to build toward the heavenly ways develops his arrogant scheme within the focus's immediate narrative.
Mockers being enclosed by what they ridiculed directly supports the focus's language of consequence surrounding its agents.
Pharaoh's evil work is beautified and his scheme ends in ruin, directly tracing the plot's failure before the focus.
Repelling evil with what is better offers a moral alternative to reciprocal harmful plotting, not an explanation of the judgment scene.
It states that evildoers cannot outrun God, a general premise for the punishment that reaches Pharaoh's people.
Evil consequences striking those who earned them supports retributive return, though the enclosing image was already established.
The warning of the Day of Meeting supplies nearby judgment context for the evil punishment stated in the focus.
The erasure of believers' evil deeds is a distant positive counterpart to evil consequences enclosing Pharaoh's people.
The plotted scheme is met by God's superior counter-plan, directly illuminating the reversal of Pharaoh's plotting.
The following verse identifies the evil punishment: Pharaoh's people are exposed to the Fire and enter its severest torment.
It expressly states that an evil plot encloses only its own people, the clearest general formulation of the focus's reversal.
Those who plot evil are warned of unexpected punishment, closely supporting the threat realized against Pharaoh's people.
Mockery of the messenger is a broad antecedent to the enclosing consequence, without the focus's plotting or protection.
Avoiding the Fire gives only a general positive contrast to the evil punishment enclosing Pharaoh's people.
It confirms the gravity of hostile plotting before God, but does not state the protection or punishment outcome.
Disbelievers disputing God's signs provides nearby opposition context but adds little to the focus's plot and punishment.
The people wrong themselves by denying signs, a general moral diagnosis rather than a direct link to the focus.
Delayed punishment that cannot be turned away then encloses the mockers closely matches the focus's surrounding retribution.
The prospect of evil punishment on the Day of Resurrection reinforces the severity of the fate assigned in the focus.
Rules for private consultation do not clarify the believer's protection or Pharaoh's punishment.
Those who mocked the signs are enclosed by what they mocked, a direct pattern but redundant after earlier formulations.
God's forgiveness, acceptance of repentance, and severe punishment frame the moral alternatives surrounding the focus.
The command to evil speech and indecency does not add a focused relation to the plot or its consequence.
The sign shown to Pharaoh is narrative background but does not explain protection from his plot or his punishment.
The order to kill believers' sons reveals Pharaoh's hostile scheme, directly contextualizing the believer protected in the focus.
Its commands about sacred rites and cooperation do not clarify the focus's plot-protection reversal.
The question about earlier generations has no focused bearing on Pharaoh's plot or punishment.
Demanding the promised judgment supplies a general mockery context, not the focus's specific reversal.
The warning to guard against what lies ahead and behind is a broad preventive counterpart to later punishment.
Severe punishment and the call to mindfulness frame an alternative to the outcome of persistent wrongdoing.
The believing man from Pharaoh's people warns against killing the messenger and against promised punishment, directly locating the protected figure and plot.
A sin that encloses its earner and makes them companions of the Fire closely supports the focus's surrounding punishment image.
God's protection from Hell's punishment gives a positive counterpart to His protection of the believer in the focus.
Mockers being enclosed by their mockery directly echoes the focus's reversal, but repeats the same established pattern.
The regulation of speaking openly about wrong does not clarify the plot or the encompassing punishment.
God's nearness to the mindful and excellent is a broad positive counterpart to protecting the believer.
Pharaoh's threatened mutilation exposes his persecution of believers, supplying background for the protected believer's danger.
Truthfulness and mindfulness offer a general positive alternative but do not clarify the focus's events.
The king's inquiry into a women's scheme is a different narrative use of plotting without a relevant consequence.
Pharaoh's council plans to kill Israelite sons, directly illustrating the oppressive designs opposed by the believer's warning.
The expiation of evil deeds through charity is a remote positive contrast to the focus's evil consequence.
The call to fear God and obey the messenger is a general antecedent to avoiding the fate in the focus.
Earlier plotters receive unexpected punishment as their structure collapses, a close general pattern of failed schemes.
Replacing wrong with good before seeking forgiveness offers a constructive contrast to the plotters' destructive course.
Acknowledging God's lordship followed by a call to mindfulness is only an indirect alternative to the focus's outcome.
The absence of authority for associating partners does not clarify the plot or its punishment.
Worldly and even harsher final punishment with no protector stresses the unprotected fate opposed to the focus's deliverance.
It confirms that warnings came to Pharaoh's people, establishing the accountability before their punishment.
People despair when evil consequence reaches them for what they earned, a general and less direct retributive parallel.
The summary that certain acts are evil does not clarify the focus's plot-protection relation.
It explicitly links Pharaoh's people's denial to God seizing them for their sins, directly explaining their punitive fate.
Musa's sighting of a fire has no material connection to the focus's punishment of Pharaoh's people.
A warning against harming the she-camel and its punishment gives only a broad wrongdoing-to-punishment pattern.
It again names Pharaoh's people, their denial, and God's seizing them for sins, directly supporting the focus's retribution.
The prisoners' dreams do not clarify Pharaoh's plot or the punishment surrounding his people.
Mockers are enclosed by what they ridiculed, a close formulaic parallel that is redundant at this later rank.
God protects the righteous from the evil of that Day, a close positive counterpart to protecting the believer from their evil plotting.
The challenge to idolaters' claimed partners does not add to the focus's protection or punishment.
The command to worship so as to be mindful offers only a general preventative alternative.
Pharaoh is grouped with communities that came with sin, supporting his inclusion in a pattern of punished transgression.
Divorce and housing obligations do not clarify the focus's plot or punishment.
Seeking God's forgiveness after wrongdoing provides a positive alternative to Pharaoh's unrepentant evil course.
The statement of greatest punishment is too general to add beyond the focus's explicit evil punishment.
Guidance for the mindful is a broad preventive contrast without a direct link to the narrative.
God's protection from burning punishment closely parallels His protection of the believer, though in a different setting.
The command to persevere and remain mindful is only a broad ethical alternative to the focus's outcome.
Fear of an evil reckoning provides an accountability horizon for the evil punishment in the focus.
The warning about questions that may distress people does not clarify the focus.
Evil punishment and final loss state a general fate comparable to that assigned to Pharaoh's people.
The prayer for protection from the Fire is a general positive counterpart to the focus's punishment.
The bare naming of Pharaoh and Thamud offers no explanatory link beyond association with punished peoples.
The believers' request for forgiveness and protection from the Fire is a positive counterpart to Pharaoh's punishment.
Mindfulness expiating evil deeds gives a distant positive alternative to evil consequences returning upon their earners.
It makes recompense correspond to the evil deeds performed, supporting the focus's retributive outcome.
The book's revelation formula does not clarify the focus's plot, protection, or punishment.
Mindfulness and kinship obligations provide no focused relation to Pharaoh's plot or fate.
The prohibition of a marriage practice does not clarify the focus.
God saves the believers who were mindful, a broad but meaningful counterpart to protecting the believer in the focus.
Qarun's destruction without helpers gives a general punishment contrast, not the focus's plot-protection relation.
Self-accounting for what one sends ahead is a general preventive alternative to later retribution.
The rhetorical affirmation of God's judgment does not add a specific link to the focus.
The Day when no relative can answer for another reinforces personal accountability behind the punishment in the focus.
The description of the messenger and believers does not clarify the focus's plot or punishment.
Eternal deprivation of protector and helper underscores the finality of punishment, though without the focus's specific plot.
The opening identification of Musa's mission to Pharaoh, Haman, and Qarun establishes the immediate conflict whose plot and reversal culminate in the focus.
Pharaoh's declared intention to kill Musa exposes the murderous scheme against which the believing man intervenes and is later protected.
The believing man seeks refuge in God from every arrogant denier of the Day of Account, directly framing the divine protection he receives.
His warning that he fears the coming Day for Pharaoh's people supplies the judgment horizon for the punishment enclosing them.
He explicitly fears for them a day like the fate of former confederates, making their threatened punishment part of a recurring pattern.
The comparison with the peoples of Nuh, Ad, Thamud, and those after them expands the historical pattern of punishment invoked against Pharaoh's people.
The warning about the Day of Calling gives immediate eschatological context to the evil punishment later assigned to Pharaoh's people.
The warning of a day when they turn away with no protector from God closely contrasts the believer's protection in the focus.
The believer contrasts their call toward the Fire with his call toward God, directly articulating the opposed destinations behind the focus's outcome.
He declares the return to God and identifies the excessive as companions of the Fire, directly anticipating the punishment that then encloses Pharaoh's people.
God's support for His messengers and believers in worldly life and on the Day of witnesses generalizes the protection given to the believing man.
Faith when punishment becomes visible is declared unavailing, clarifying the irreversible moment reached by Pharaoh's people.
The opponents plot while God counter-plans more effectively, directly illuminating how a hostile scheme fails to overcome the protected believer.
Earlier people plotted, but the entire plan belongs to God and every soul will know what it earned, joining failed plotting to recompense.
Those who devise a plot are met by God's counter-plan while unaware, a close structural parallel to the focus's reversal.
The outcome of their plot is that they and their people are destroyed, directly showing a scheme returning destructively upon its authors.
A man warns Musa that the chiefs are plotting to kill him and urges escape, directly paralleling the Pharaoh court's threat context.
Pharaoh and his troops are seized and cast into the sea for arrogance and denial, directly supplying a punitive outcome for the same party.
God takes vengeance on Pharaoh's people by drowning them for denying signs, directly clarifying their historical punishment.
Pharaoh's final drowning after pursuing the Children of Israel supplies the decisive historical punishment of his party.
Pharaoh's belief only after disobedience and corruption underscores the futility of recognition once punishment has arrived.
The preservation of Pharaoh's body as a sign gives the punitive outcome an enduring warning function.
After Pharaoh seeks to expel Musa and his people, God drowns him and those with him, directly reversing his hostile design.
The sea overwhelms Pharaoh as he pursues Musa's people, directly depicting the punishment of the pursuing plotter.
Pharaoh and his forces are taken and cast into the sea while blameworthy, a concise direct statement of their retribution.
God seizes Pharaoh with the exemplary punishment of the last and first, reinforcing the severity of the fate named in the focus.
Pharaoh leads his people into the Fire on the Day of Resurrection, directly extending the focus's punishment of Pharaoh's people into final judgment.
A curse follows Pharaoh and his people in this world and the Day of Resurrection, reinforcing the lasting scope of their punishment.
